Objectives:
The objective of the proposed action is to re-establish sagebrush cover in areas
burned by the 2007 Murphy Complex Fire that are currently dominated by native perennial
grasses, including bluebunch wheatgrass (Pseudoroegneria spicata), Idaho fescue (Festuca
idahoensis), bottlebrush squirreltail (Elymus elymoides), and Sandbergs bluegrass (Poa secunda).
Planned_Implementation:
Bare-root or containerized Wyoming big sagebrush seedlings would be hand-planted in early spring and mid- to late fall. Holes would be dug using hand tools such as planting bars, resulting in a disturbance area of about 2-3 inches diameter. Shrub seedlings would be planted in patches of about 200-500 plants. Patches would generally be oriented in a north-south arrangement to facilitate natural dispersal of seed by wind. Shrub seedlings would be spaced no closer than 3 feet
from each other, and placed at least 3 feet from existing, live mature or seedling shrubs, including rabbitbrush (Ericameria nauseosa or Chrysothamnus viscidiflorus). Shrubs could be placed less than 3 feet from dead sagebrush for sun and wind protection and to access soil nutrients and mycorrhizal fungi that are associated with areas under sagebrush canopies. Shrub seedlings would not be planted in areas with obvious existing populations of invasive plants (primarily cheatgrass,
Bromus tectorum) or noxious weeds to reduce potential for competition or unintentional herbicide treatment.
Clearing of Planting Spot (Hand Scalping) - The planting spot may be exposed mineral soil or covered with
vegetation, gravel or slash, which will require a clearing effort before planting. Clearing shall include the removal
of all debris, gravel, humus, ash, dead vegetation material and living vegetation (including surface roots) a
minimum of two inches deep. Cleared areas shall be no smaller than 12 inches in diameter. There shall be a
minimum of six inches of cleared space surrounding planted seedling, i.e. the seedling shall be planted near the
center of the 12-inch cleared area. Wherever possible or practical, locate spots on the north and east sides of
stumps, logs, and rocks.
Actual_Implementation: 150,000 Wyoming big sagebrush were planted in the planned area.

Planned_Implementation:
In order to restore sagebrush for sage-grouse it is proposed to plant Wyoming big
sagebrush plugs and/or bare root seedlings in key areas on 26,000 acres. Approximately 435
plants would be planted every acre to re-establish Wyoming big sagebrush habitat within the
burned area. Potential planting areas were selected based on 1) presence of Wyoming big
sagebrush prior to the fire, 2) habitat that has the potential to grow sagebrush, 3) presence
of PPH, and 4) areas identified by Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife as a priority for
sagebrush restoration. Inventory of the populations of sagebrush in 2013 will help identify
specific areas where Wyoming big sagebrush communities were consumed by the fire.
These locations would be planted in 2014. Hand planting of the Wyoming sagebrush gives a
greater chance of success for the plants to get established within the first year after
planting. The plantings will consist of using hand tools to dig small holes to plant the
seedlings.

Trt_Concerns_Desc: The BLM has made the determination that as a result of the Holloway Fire, affected vegetative communities, particularly sage brush communities within Sage Grouse Preliminary Priority Habitat (PPH) and Preliminary General Habitat (PGH), are at risk from long term habitat degradation due to the presence of invasive annual grasses and other noxious weeds within new\r\ndisturbance. Objectives: Establish native shrubs within the burn perimeter in order to re-establish sage grouse habitat and restore proper ecosystem structure and function. Over 20% plug survival would be considered successful.
Planned_Implementation: Due to poor success rates of sagebrush establishing from seeding treatments, coupled with encouraging results from plug seeding treatments from the EOARC (Eastern Oregon Agriculture Research Center), and others, we\u2019ve chosen to attempt to get more funding for plug seeding than purchasing of sagebrush seed to be applied in initial seeding treatments. It is the Burns BLM I.D. teams conclusion (based upon local research, experience, and knowledge) that planting sagebrush plugs offers the highest chance to reestablish sagebrush for obligate species such as sage-grouse and pygmy rabbits.
Actual_Implementation:
FY13:
A contract was awarded to collect Wyoming big sagebrush seed from on district in order to have
a local seed for growing out plugs to plant in out years. This contract was done with BAR
funding, as well as Seeds of Success (L10100000) funding. During the contracting phase, the
government estimate was established and was only able to fund collection of 30 pounds of pure
live seed. However, when the contract bids came in, they were well under the government
estimate. Therefore, more than 2/3 of the money allocated to this was not spent. The majority
of the remaining money from this was applied to the weed contract (with SO/WO approval) to
help cover R5 costs in FY2014, with a small portion of it going to the fence reconstruction
contract. Seed collection should occur in the late fall of 2013. UPDATE FY2014: Seed
collection did occur in 2013; however, the viability of the seed was not expected to be high due
to drought conditions so alternative local seed sources were found for seedling grow-out.

FY14:
The funding request for this treatment was substantially decreased from what had been planned
in order to provide a more realistic estimate of what was would be able to be spent due to the
high demand for sagebrush seedlings. While the requested amount was originally allocated to
this treatment, there was still concern that Lucky Peak Nursery would not be able to meet all of
their demands. In addition, the Burns District discovered a fence that needed to be fully
reconstructed and needed to reallocate some funding to that effort. Therefore, only $75,000 was
applied to the interagency agreement with Lucky Peak Nursery.
Lucky Peak Nursery will be growing out seedlings over the next fiscal year, which should be
ready to plant in Spring or Fall of 2015.

FY15:
The contract to plant sagebrush seedlings was awarded for $422,985, which was less than
expected. The additional amount was spent on contract administration, including project
inspection throughout the period of performance of the contract, including overtime for BLM
employees. Approximately 2,930 acres within the Miller Homestead perimeter were planted
with sagebrush seedlings at a rate of approximately 440 seedlings per acre. Subsequent
monitoring has shown good success in many of the seedling areas.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Seedling Planting (R4)
Objective: Establish native shrubs within the burn perimeter in order to re-establish sage grouse habitat and restore proper ecosystem
structure and function. Over 20% plug survival would be considered successful.
In fall 2015 and spring 2016, approximately 1,163,000 Wyoming big sagebrush seedlings were planted within
the Miller Homestead Fire perimeter. These seedlings were planted in twelve different units. Prior to 2017, the
only monitoring that occurred was related to areas that overlapped with existing trend plots, and monitoring of
the contracted planters. In 2017, a crew was used to establish belt transects within 10 of the 12-planted units to
document sagebrush density in these units. In addition, a second transect was established outside of the planted
area to compare planted sagebrush seedlings with areas of natural recovery. At each location, all sagebrush
plants within a 100m by 2m belt were recorded, with an age class determined. Four belts, one in each cardinal
direction, was completed at each location. The densities shown in the tables below are all number of plants per
0.02 ha, and show the range provided across the four belts.

Plot ID's:
[6001-001-IN UTM 319168 E X 4739036 N], [DVJM-UPSH-102-OUT UTM 319523 E X 4738921 N]
This pair of plots shows some establishment in the planted area, however, more sagebrush plants are
found outside the planted area. Due to the high density of mature sagebrush plants at this location, it is
expected that this are outside of the seeded area did not burn as completely as some other plot locations.

[6029-ESR18-IN UTM 326841 E X 4750501 N], [LMF20144125313119B3-OUT UTM 327696E X 4749566 N]
With this pair of plots, some level of success in sagebrush planting is seen, as there is a density up to
550 plants/0.02 ha, while there are no sagebrush plants found outside of the seedling area. This does
suggest that natural recovery of sagebrush may be minimal in this area.

[6111-ESR31-IN UTM 335041 E X 4749752 N], [6029-ESR31-OUT UTM 334420 E X 4750651 N]
There was no success within this planted area. There is also no natural recovery occurring. This area
may need additional sagebrush treatments in the future to ensure sagebrush becomes established.

[7001-ESR01-IN UTM 341457 E X 4765996 N], [7001-007-OUT UTM 342932 E X 4765404 N]
These plots show good survival of planted sagebrush seedlings, which are establishing a seed source in
the area. Some natural recovery is also occurring in the area, outside of the planted area, which will
further increase the sagebrush seedbank and promote good recovery.

[7001-ESR02-IN UTM 336237 E X 4766214 N], [7001-ESR02-OUT UTM 337173 E X 4767127 N]
Due to the large number of mature plants, it is possible that there was a good amount of sagebrush
survival following the fire, both in the planted area and outside the planted area. Additional inventory of
the site prior to designating the unit for planting seedlings may have allowed us to select another area
with fewer or no mature sagebrush plants. However, there is a good density of both seedling and
juvenile plants, suggesting the planted sagebrush may have been successful.

[7001-ESR07-IN UTM 343575 E X 4758282 N], [7001-ESR07-OUT UTM 344560 E X 4759390 N]
The belt transect within the planted area suggests there is a minimal level of success and plants should
mature and produce seed in this area. No natural recovery seems to be taking place in the area. This site
should continue to be monitored and may be a potential location of future treatments.

Monitoring suggests that out of the 10 units monitored, there was some level of success, seen by the presence of
surviving sagebrush plants, in seven of the units; three units show failure. However, as only one plot was
monitored in each of the ten units, there may be success in other portions of the units. In addition, six of the 10
out of planted area plots show some sagebrush plants present. This suggests that in many areas, some degree of
natural recovery is occurring. In order to get a better picture of sagebrush survival on the landscape, the Burns
District has an assistance agreement to utilize on the ground photos with remote sensing to estimate sagebrush
cover. The original inventory using this method was completed in 2016. A follow up inventory in the next 5 to
10 years should show the success/failure of planting within these units by comparing the shrub cover in the
units to that outside of the units.

Objectives: The objective of the proposed action is to re-establish bitterbrush cover in areas burned by the 2007 Murphy Complex Fire that are currently dominated by native perennial grasses, including bluebunch wheatgrass (Pseudoroegneria spicata) and Idaho fescue (Festuca idahoensis). This planting is proposed to enhance and accelerate recovery of brood-rearing habitat for sage-grouse, a candidate for listing under the Endangered Species Act (ESA), as well as crucial mule deer winter range.
Planned_Implementation: Bare-root or containerized antelope bitterbrush seedlings would be hand-planted in early spring and mid- to late fall. Holes would be dug using hand tools such as planting bars, resulting in a disturbance area of about 2-3 inches diameter. Shrub seedlings would be planted in patches of about 100-1,000 plants throughout the proposed planting areas. Shrub seedlings would be spaced no closer than 3 feet from each other, and placed at least 3 feet from existing, live mature or seedling shrubs, including rabbitbrush (Ericameria nauseosa or Chrysothamnus viscidiflorus). Shrubs could be placed less than 3 feet from dead shrub skeletons for sun and wind protection and to access soil nutrients and mycorrhizal fungi that are associated with areas under shrub canopies. Shrub seedlings would not be planted in areas with obvious existing populations of invasive plants (primarily cheatgrass, Bromus tectorum) or noxious weeds to reduce potential for competition or unintentional herbicide treatment.\r\nFull-size vehicles would be restricted to existing roads. Limited temporary use of off-road vehicles such as all-terrain vehicles (ATVs) could be used to access remote planting locations. Limited use would be implemented in a manner such that tracks to and from planting locations would have low visibility and impacts to soils and vegetation would be minimal or negligible. This would include locating staging areas on rocky or otherwise hardened areas and using different routes for ingress and egress. Temporary travel corridors would be identified prior to implementation for specific planting locations.\r\nSpring planting activities would not occur until after 9 a.m. to reduce potential disturbance to sage-grouse. Planting would not occur within 300 feet of a major travel route, 50 feet of any two-track road or fenceline, or during muddy or saturated soil conditions. Under agreement between the Bureau and the State Historic Preservation Officer, cultural resource inventory is not required for compliance with Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act for hand planting projects. However, the Jarbidge Field Office Archeologist will identify avoidance areas prior to planting activities and would be notified immediately should artifacts be found during implementation of the planting project. Fuels program specialists would be on-site to insure implementation of planting restrictions.

Objectives: The Saddle Draw Fire greatly reduced the abundance of Wyoming big sagebrush and bitterbrush in the fire area. Wyoming big sagebrush is required component for sagebrush obligate species such as sage-grouse. Bitterbrush is an important browse species for big game animals during winter. Restoring the sagebrush and bitterbrush cover that was removed by the fire will speed the recovery and rehabilitation of sage-grouse and big game habitats in the fire area.
Planned_Implementation:
Sagebrush Seedling Planting:
In order to restore sagebrush for sage-grouse it is proposed to plant sagebrush seedling plugs in key areas, including near lek sites. There are 10 leks that are located within the fire perimeter. Areas to plant sagebrush seedlings were prioritized based upon proximity to a lek, land ownership, soil type and potential for seedlings to be able to establish on the site. Eight
of the ten leks that occur in the fire area are on private land. Other sagebrush seeding methods are being proposed as part of this plan. Seedlings would be planted in small groups separated by areas that would not be planted. This will allow the seedlings to be planted over a larger area. The small areas of seedlings would provide a seed source for the future
expansion of sagebrush in the fire area. Locally adapted seed would be collected and grown out to produce the sagebrush seedlings. The use of local sagebrush seed for the seedlings would assure that the plants that are planted out would be adapted to the site and would establish and produce more seed. This treatment will use local native seed as the source for
the seedlings in compliance with WO IM-2014-114.
Bitterbrush Seedling Planting
A significant portion of old growth bitterbrush was consumed by the fire. Based on sage grouse lek locations, this area provided important cover for sage grouse, as well as providing important forage for wildlife, including mule deer, elk and antelope. In addition, 2000 acres of Antelope bitterbrush seedlings are proposed for planting. Local native bitterbrush seed would be collected and used to grow the plugs giving the seedlings the local genetics needed to survive these harsh sites. Seedlings would be planted in small groups separated by areas that would not be planted. This will allow the seedlings to be
planted over a larger area. The small areas of seedlings would provide a seed source for the future expansion of sagebrush in the fire area. The areas planted with bitterbrush seedlings would be protected from wildlife and livestock with an eight foot protective fence. Vexar tubes were considered but the Burns District has had poor success with these. The animals
pull off the unstacked vexar and eat the seedlings.
For all seedling plantings:
Proposed restoration activities involving seedling plantings are considered undertakings warranting review and compliance with Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act. This work needs to be conducted in consultation with the State Historic Preservation Officer, affected Indian tribes and others as appropriate. BLM is developing specific plans for conducting archaeological survey and site identification services focusing on emergency stabilization of burned areas including seedling plantings where these activities have the potential to affect cultural properties. It is cautiously estimated that all 4,000 acres of proposed seedling plantings areas will require cultural resources inventory at some level for the Saddle Draw Fire Recovery Project. The fire area is a checkerboard of private, state, and BLM managed lands. Thus, cadastral surveys will be required of ground disturbing treatment areas to avoid trespass treatment of other land ownerships.

Seedling planting started after the first rains of the fall. The cost of
growing the seedlings and planting the seedlings was paid for with
FY 16 funding. Cost for PI work was paid for with FY 17 funding.
Treatment monitoring will occur this fall, to give the plants a full
year of growing before assessing success.

Of the total planted Nevada Division of Wildlife donated 52,000 seedlings. The majority of
the seedlings were sowed in May of 2014 at the USDA Forest Service, Lucky Peak Nursery
located in Boise, ID. The Winnemucca staff sent seeds to the nursery that was collected from
similar seed zones to those found within the Winnemucca District. The three post fire areas
are the Thomas, Hanson, and Holloway fires. The 2007 Thomas Fire occurred just outside of
town near Water Canyon, and roughly 21,000 Wyoming sagebrush seedlings were installed.
The Hanson and Holloway Fires both occurred in 2012. The Hanson Fire area had roughly
33,000 Wyoming sagebrush seedlings installed. In the Holloway Fire area we planted at
three different locations within the area for a total of 18,500 antelope bitterbrush,
36,500 mountain sagebrush, and 19,000 Wyoming sagebrush. The entire project was
completed in 10 days by hand installation using hoe-dads. Refer to map 5 and table 5 in part
12 Attachments.

While seedling planting is historically more expensive than direct
seeding, this project makes efficient use of sagebrush (and other shrub) seed which is
supply-limited. Hand installment of shrubs also allows for greater probability of overall
treatment success since viable microsites can be identified and targeted for planting. When
probability of success and recent price-increase of sagebrush seed, and required seed
volumes for direct seeding are factored in, handplanting is cost-competitive with direct
seeding, is less likely to be detrimentally affected by seed shortages, and can be successfully
implemented outside of the first season seeding window.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
A few small, unburned islands of sagebrush within
the fire perimeter may provide short-term refuge for some sage-grouse, but the wildfire killed the vast majority of
sagebrush plants. The burned area now provides virtually no cover and forage for this species. Most individuals
that survived the fire and avoided predation immediately after the fire have been displaced into sagebrush steppe
outside the fire perimeter. Sage-grouse may find limited forage near the edge of the fire, but most individuals are
expected to avoid the area, especially during the winter months, until the sagebrush recovers to the extent it once
again provides adequate hiding cover and forage. Sage-grouse have been observed returning to leks in burned areas
in subsequent seasons, but the size of the area burned in the Soda fire and distance to sagebrush cover would be
expected to diminish or possibly eliminate use of existing leks in the burned area for several years or decades.

Planned_Implementation: Shrub seedlings would be planted in patches of about 200-500 plants throughout the burned area. Patches would generally be oriented in a north-south arrangement to facilitate natural dispersal of seed by wind. Shrub seedlings would be spaced no closer than 3 feet from each other, and placed at least 3 feet from existing, live mature or seedling shrubs. Shrubs could be placed less than 3 feet from dead sagebrush for sun and wind protection and to access soil nutrients and mycorrhizal fungi that are associated with areas under sagebrush canopies.

Objectives: When planting or reseeding sagebrush, favor the sagebrush species, subspecies, that are appropriate for the ecological site. Source identified seed is preferable. To maximize the likelihood of establishment, consider multiple approaches, such as aerial seeding, ground broadcast seeding with harrow or roller, and planting of seedlings in strategic patches or strips. Avoid seeding sagebrush or other shrubs near road margins if the road and road margin might otherwise serve as a fuel break in the event of future fire.
Planned_Implementation:
3.3 PLANTING METHODS
A. The following requirements will apply to all planting units, unless identified otherwise.
B. Proper selection of planting site is important to provide protection from animal damage, sun, wind, loose debris,
and other agents detrimental to seedling survival and growth.
C. Plant spacing will be 8-15 feet and plants will be planted in large groups utilizing a grid pattern by planting crews.
Planting grid patterns must cover the entire planting project unit with exceptions for avoidance areas (see section
H below) or as allowed by the Project Inspector due to site conditions.
D. Plants will be placed no closer than 3 feet away from existing live brush plants, but could be placed closer to
standing dead shrubs.
E. Clearing efforts will be required to prepare the site for planting and maintaining required spacing.
F. An unplantable area (spot) will be indicated by the Project Inspector prior to planting on the project site. The
Project Inspector will make the determination whether a site is plantable or unplantable.
G. Where an unplantable spot is encountered: The planter shall move over the unplantable spot and plant in the
closest plantable spot available, and then resume required spacing. Examples of unplantables are:
1. Rock outcrops, talus slopes, and areas of stone, cobbles or gravel that is 12" deep.
2. Sites with obvious rodent or insect (ant hill) activity.
3. Sites with obvious run-off, i.e. bottom of drainages.
4. Animal & human travel paths - planting sites shall be a minimum of five feet, each side, from travel paths.
5. Within .25 miles of livestock troughs or supplement sites.
6. Within 50. feet of two-track roads or fence lines.
7. Within 300 feet of main travel roads.
8. Cultural avoidance areas as identified on the project maps.
H. Planting will not occur on slick spots where they exist, or near other sensitive areas.
I. For tracking shrub survival, monitoring points will be installed by Government representatives at every project
site. The number of monitoring points will be directly related to project size (acres treated/planted) and given to
the Contractor prior to the start of planting. The guidelines are as follows:
1. Two stakes (start and end) will be installed by Government representatives prior to planting. Transect length
will be 300', using a tape to measure the distance.
2. Two planters, provided by the Contractor or Sub-contractor, will plant one seedling every 6' of the tape,
alternating on both sides on the tape, starting at O' .
3. Planters will need to plant seedlings no further than 3' from the tape.
4. The total amount of seedlings planted at each monitoring point will be 50 seedlings (25 on the left side of the
tape, 25 on the right side of the tape).

3.4 SEEDLING PLACEMENT
A. Consolidated Containerized Seedling Planting - The seedling shall be suspended near the center of the hole with
roots extending down in a near natural arrangement at a depth that, after filling, packing, and leveling, the root
collar is even with or slightly below the firmed soil level. No portion of the roots shall be exposed. If an auger is
used, seedlings shall be planted in the center of the augured hole. Planting on the side of the hole will not be
permitted. Only one seedling may be planted per hole, multiple seedlings planted in a single hole will be
considered wasted and may result in assessment of liquidated damages against the Contractor (see Payment
Section).
B. Filling and Firming- Moist mineral soil shall be filled in and firmed around seedling roots. Dry soil, ash, organic
matter, rocks, and other foreign matter shall be kept out of holes. Soil shall be filled in and firmed progressively
(layered) so no loose soil or air pockets remain and the seedling is as firmly planted as soil conditions allow. The
Contractor shall not wedge the seedl1ng in the side of the hole. Firming the soil around the seedling shall be done
in a manner that assures the seedling and root systems are not damaged. After the soil is firmed around the
seedling, it shall be smoothed out to the level horizontal to surrounding soil surface. See Attachment. After
planting the seedlings the stem shall stand erect. The seedling shall not be wedged down with mud or debris. Soil
or other debris shall not be left covering the leaves or stems of the planted seedling.

Objectives: re-establish sagebrush cover in areas burned by wildfires over the past decade
Planned_Implementation: the original size of the project unit was 13,418 acres.\r\nContainerized or bare root shrub seedlings would be hand-planted in early spring and/or mid- to late fall. Holes would be dug using hand tools such as planting bars and hoe-dads, resulting in a disturbance area of about 3 inches diameter. Shrub seedlings would be planted in patches of about 500-1000 plants. Patches would generally be oriented in a north-south arrangement to facilitate natural dispersal of seed by wind. Shrub seedlings would be spaced no closer than 10 feet from each other, and placed at least 10 feet from existing, live mature or seedling shrubs, including rabbitbrush (Ericameria nauseosa or Chrysothamnus viscidiflorus). Shrubs could be placed less than 10 feet from dead sagebrush for sun and wind protection and to access soil nutrients and mycorrhizal fungi that are associated with areas under sagebrush canopies. Shrub seedlings would not be planted in areas with obvious existing populations of invasive plants (primarily cheatgrass, Bromus tectorum) or noxious weeds to reduce potential for competition or unintentional herbicide treatment. Seedlings would not be planted in slickspot microsites, if present.

See the attached map for the project location.\r\nThe contractor was Loy G. Pehrson of Darlington, ID. The sub-contractor for the planting portion of the contract was MP Forestry of Bend, OR. Foreman for the planting crew was Enrique Moreno. Crew numbers consisted of 27 planters. The project was completed using hoedads and UTV\u2019s for transporting seedlings. Grassy Hills was monitoring on June 6th, 2016. Seedlings looked healthy, with no yellowing or leaf loss.
The average survival rate was low, at 10%. This could be due to several factors. Note the container size
for this project area versus the other project areas. While the 6 cubic inch seedling is favored because
it’s easier to plant with lower incidence of j-rooting, it’s easier to get in rocky and clay soils, and the root
mass in these particular seedlings was vigorous, their size may be linked to the low rates. The length in
the 10 cubic inch gives the seedlings that extra length it needs for its roots to reach readily available
water sources through the lower and upper soil levels. However, these seedlings have a higher tendency
to be planted incorrectly (j-rooting) if not thoroughly mitigated.
However, these factors must also be taken into account: These were planted in early November, just
before and during snowfall; seedlings were planted in rough and rocky soils, making it hard for planters
to get a decent depth with their hand tools; the seedlings are competing for root space with existing
perennial grasses and herbs; seedlings can go through an initial shock once planted, which makes them
appear dead when they’re in a dormant stage. We documented live seedlings from previous planting
projects that exhibited this behavior. Overall, seedling survival rate for the 2015 planting season
appeared to be much higher/more successful than years past. Initial observations in early Spring 2016
showed a very high survival rate (at least 80%) before the rise in temperatures and drop in relative
humidity.

3.1 SEEDLING PREPARATION
A. The Contractor shall be responsible for removal of seedlings from the container prior to planting.
B. The Contractor shall be responsible for empty seedling containers and site clean up after planting is complete. C. Contractor will be required to consolidate and organize used cones for quick removal after planting, as well as
boxes and other materials used to transport seedlings

A. Preparing the Planting Hole- Planting holes shall be located near the center of the prepared area and shall be oriented at an angle between perpendicular to the slope and true vertical (see Attachment). Planting spots may be cleared (scalped) a maximum of 24 hours prior to plant hole preparation. Planting hole must be two inches deeper than the maximum root length of the seedlings. Plant hole shall be prepared (dug) a maximum of one hour prior to planting the seedling

A. Microsite/Standard Shade Specification Planting - The following requirements will apply to all planting units, unless identified otherwise.
B. Seedlings will be planted in accordance with the Microsite/Standard Shade Specification planting method whenever possible. Proper selection of planting site is important to provide protection from animal damage, sun, wind, loose debris, and other agents detrimental to seedling survival and growth. Planting spots shall be selected where the Standard Shade Specification planting method (stationary shade) protection sources are located. The largest material or feature available is preferred as the protection source. The seedling shall be planted as close as possible, but not more than six inches away from the protection source. Seedlings shall be planted on the northern (northwest to northeast) sides of stationary material. When transportable or stationary material is not available for protection the seedling shall be planted with the Standard Planting method. Planters will be required to plant all areas, unless they meet one or more of the conditions defined below as unplantable.
C. Plant Spacing will be 8-15 feet and plants will be planted in large groups of 500-1500 plants, or depending on micro-site suitability, but no less than 500 plants per site.
D. Plants will be placed no closer than 3' feet away from existing live brush plants, but could be placed closer to standing dead shrubs.
E. The prescribed spacing shall be varied up to 50% to take advantage of a suitable planting spot with existing stationary shade. Shrubs not properly placed to take advantage of existing stationary shade will receive a planting spot selection deduction for the above ground inspection. However, if suitable stationary shade is not available within the 50% variance of the prescribed spacing, planting spot selection shall be based entirely on the
prescribed spacing requirements.
F. Standard Planting- Proper selection of planting site is important, and clearing efforts will be required to prepare the site for planting and maintaining required spacing. Examples of plantable and unplantable areas in this method will be indicated by the Project Inspector on the project site.
G. An unplantable area (spot) will be indicated by the Project Inspector prior to planting on the project site.
The Project Inspector will make the determination whether a site is plantable or unplantable.
H. Where an unplantable spot is encountered: The planter shall move over the unplantable spot and plant in the closest plantable spot available, and then resume required spacing. Examples of unplantables are:
1. Rock outcrops, talus slopes, and areas of stone, cobbles or gravel over 12" deep.
2. Sites with obvious rodent activity.
3. Sites with obvious run-off, i.e. very bottoms of drainages.
4. Animal & human travel paths - planting sites shall be a minimum of five feet, each side, from travel paths.
5. Within .25 miles of livestock troughs or supplement sites.
6. Within 50 feet of two-track roads or fence lines.
7. Within 300 feet of main travel roads.
I. Planting will not occur on slick spots where they exist, or near other sensitive areas.

3.4 SEEDLING PLACEMENT
A. Consolidated Containerized Seedling Planting - The seedling shall be suspended near the center of the hole with roots extending down in a near natural arrangement at a depth that, after filling, packing, and leveling, the root collar is even with or slightly below the firmed soil level. No portion of the roots shall be exposed. If an auger is used, seedlings shall be planted in the center of the augered hole. Planting on the side of the hole will not be permitted.
B. Filling and Firming - Moist mineral soil shall be filled in and firmed around seedling roots. Dry soil, ash, organic matter, rocks, and other foreign matter shall be kept out of holes. Soil shall be filled in and firmed progressively (layered) so no loose soil or air pockets remain and the seedling is as firmly planted as soil conditions will allow. Filling planting holes and firming is done in three phases: Filling the hole 1/3 to 1/2 full and compacting, filling the hole 2/3 full and compacting, and completion of filling and compacting. The Contractor shall not wedge the seedling in the side of the hole. Firming the soil around the seedling shall be done in a manner that assures the seedling and root systems are not damaged. After the soil is firmed around the seedling it shall be smoothed out to the level horizontal to surrounding soil surface. See Attachment. After planting the seedling the stem shall stand erect. The seedling shall not be wedged down with mud or debris. Soil or other debris shall not be left covering the leaves or stems of the planted seedling.
C. Auxiliary Hole - An auxiliary hole is a hole dug on the edge of the 12-inch diameter cleared area to obtain additional soil to assist in the refilling and firming of soil around the seedling or an attempted hole that did not meet the minimum depth required for seedling planting. These may be dug but shall be refilled with soil or debris.

Trt_Concerns_Desc: The proposed actions is to plant approximately 50,000 Wyoming big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata spp. wyomingensis) seedlings to re-establish shrub cover in an area burned by the Murphy Complex Fire in August, 2007. This supplemental planting is proposed to enhance and accelerate recovery of these shrub communities and habitat for sage-grouse, other sagebrush-obligate wildlife, and special status plants, including slickspot peppergrass (Lepidium papilliferum). Location of the proposed project is intended to enhance connectivity between existing key sage-grouse habitats.

Objectives: Bare-root or containerized Wyoming big sagebrush seedlings would be hand-planted.
Planned_Implementation: Holes would be dug using hand tools such as planting bars, resulting in a disturbance area of about 203 inches diameter. Shrub seedlings would be planted in areas between strips of sagebrush seedlings resulting from ESR treatments. Shrub seedlings would not be planted in areas with obvious existing populations of invasive plants (primarily cheatgrass, Bromus tectorum) or noxious weeds to reduce potential for competition or unintentional herbicide treatment. The identified planting area is about 4,300 acres. Shrub seedlings would be planted in patches of about 200-500 plants to facilitate future natural distribution of seed. Shrub seedlings would be spaced not closer than 3 feet apart, and placed at least 3 feet from existing, live mature or seedling sagebrush or rabbitbrush. Shrubs could be places less than 3 feet from dead sagebrush for sun and wind protection and to access soil nutrients and mycorrhizal fungi that are associated with areas under sagebrush canopies. Vehicles would be restricted to existing roads. Planting would not occur within 0.25 mile of livestock water or supplement locations, within 50 feet of any two-track road or fenceline, within 300 feet of main graveled roads, or during saturated soil conditions. Planting would not occur in slickspot microsites. Under agreement with the Bureau and the State Historic Preservation Officer, cultural resource inventory is not required for compliance with Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act for hand planting projects. However, the Jarbidge Field Office Archeologist would be notified immediately should artifacts be found during implementation of the planting project. Fuels program specialists would be on-site the first day of planting to provide guidance to the contractor regarding planting restrictions.

3.2 SITE PREPARATION
A. Preparing the Planting Hole - Planting holes shall be located near the center of the prepared area and shall be
oriented at an angle between perpendicular to the slope and true vertical (see Attachment). Planting hole must be
two inches deeper than the maximum root length of the seedlings.
3 .3 PLANTING METHODS
A. The following requirements will apply to all planting units, unless identified otherwise.
B. Proper selection of planting site is important to provide protection from animal damage, sun, wind, loose debris,
and other agents detrimental to seedling survival and growth.
C. Plant spacing will be 8-15 feet and plants will be planted in large groups utilizing a grid pattern by planting crews.
Planting grid patterns must cover the entire planting project unit with exceptions for avoidance areas (see section
H below) or as allowed by the Project Inspector due to site conditions.
D. Plants will be placed no closer than 3 feet away from existing live brush plants, but could be placed closer to
standing dead shrubs.
E. Clearing efforts will be required to prepare the site for planting and maintaining required spacing.
F. An unplantable area (spot) will be indicated by the Project Inspector prior to planting on the project site. The
Project Inspector will make the determination whether a site is plantable or unplantable.
G. Where an unplantable spot is encountered: The planter shall move over the unplantable spot and plant in the
closest plantable spot available, and then resume required spacing. Examples unplantable are:
1. Rock outcrops, talus slopes, and areas of stone, cobbles or gravel that is 12" deep.
2. Sites with obvious rodent or insect (ant hill) activity.
3. Sites with obvious run-off, i.e. bottom of drainages.
4. Animal & human travel paths - planting sites shall be a minimum of five feet, each side, from travel paths.
5. Within .25 miles of livestock troughs or supplement sites.
6. Within 50 feet of two-track roads or fence lines.
7. Within 300 feet of main travel roads.
8. Cultural avoidance areas as identified on the project maps.
H. Planting will not occur on slick spots where they exist, or near other sensitive areas.

3.4 SEEDLING PLACEMENT
A. Consolidated Containerized Seedling Planting - The seedling shall be suspended near the center of the hole with
roots extending down in a near natural arrangement at a depth that, after filling, packing, and leveling, the root
collar is even with or slightly below the firmed soil level. No portion of the roots shall be exposed. If an auger is
used, seedlings shall be planted in the center of the augured hole. Planting on the side of the hole will not be
permitted. Only one seedling may be planted per hole, multiple seedlings planted in a single hole will be
considered wasted and may result in assessment of liquidated damages against the Contractor (see Payment
Section).
B. Filling and Firming - Moist mineral soil shall be filled in and firmed around seedling roots. Dry soil, ash, organic
matter, rocks, and other foreign matter shall be kept out of holes. Soil shall be filled in and firmed progressively
(layered) so no loose soil or air pockets remain and the seedling is as firmly planted as soil conditions allow. The
Contractor shall not wedge the seedling in the side of the hole. Firming the soil around the seedling shall be done
in a manner that assures the seedling and root systems are not damaged. After the soil is firmed around the
seedling, it shall be smoothed out to the level horizontal to surrounding soil surface. See Attachment. After
planting the seedlings the stem shall stand erect. The seedling shall not be wedged down with mud or debris. Soil
or other debris shall not be left covering the leaves or stems of the planted seedling.
3.5 SEEDLING CARE - SEED CACHES (TEMPORARY STORAGE)
\xb7 A. A Government Official shall approve all seedling caches or temporary storage sites. Overnight storage will be
cleared by the Government Official/COR. . (
B. Temporary seedling caches shall be covered with seedling protection tarps (heat shields) approved by a
Government Official and furnished by the contractor.
C. Seedlings stored in boxes, bags, or bundles shall not be exposed to direct sunlight. Punctured or tom bags or
boxes must be promptly resealed. Containers of seedlings shall be opened only in full shade.

Trt_Concerns_Desc: The vegetation communities within the fire boundary are dominated by juniper, medusahead and cheatgrass due to several previous fires. The fire area is at risk for full conversion to an annual dominated rangeland, which would greatly reduce the productivity of the site for wildlife and livestock, increasing the potential for future erosion and the risk for more frequent and intense wildfires. Most weeds recover more quickly than native or other non-native desirable perennials, taking advantage of moisture and nutrients earlier, and proliferate following wildfire. No previous seedings or treatments of medusahead or cheatgrass were performed at the time of any historic fires due to the inability to implement treatment of aerial herbicide applications of imazapic. Very few sites within the fire contain Wyoming big sagebrush, bitterbrush, rabbit brush, bluebunch wheatgrass, bluegrass species, hawksbeard, milkvetch, and balsamroot. The majority of the live juniper were not killed by the fire. Other known noxious weed infestations in the fire area are Scotch thistle, whitetop, Russian and spotted knapweed. There is also potential for other noxious weeds that are documented in close proximity to the fire area to move into the fire perimeter.\r\n\r\nResource concerns within the burned area include maintenance of native perennial and desirable non-native species and expansion of existing weeds, especially medusahead and cheatgrass. Proposed emergency stabilization and rehabilitation (ESR) treatments and actions include herbicide treatment, aerial seeding, and monitoring.

Planned_Implementation:
1. This unit is divided into 2 types of big sagebrush sites for planting Wyoming Big Sagebrush.
2. Big sagebrush sites defined below:
a. Mounded sites are intermixed with low sagebrush. These sites range in size from small approximately 1 yd2 to large 5 to 10 yd2.
i. Small Mounds plant 2 seedlings per mound.
ii. Large Mounds plant 9 seedlings with 1 in the middle and the other 8 in a circle, 2 paces from the middle and from one another.
iii. Avoid planting in low areas with ponded water, these are low sage sites and big sagebrush will die in these areas.
b. Level sites predominately on the western 2/3 of the unit.
i. Plant 9 seedlings with 1 in the middle and the other 8 in a circle, 2 paces from the middle and from one another.
ii. Then take 20 to 30 paces (20 yards) to next area to plant and repeat planting another 9 seedlings. This method should plant about 140 seedlings per acre.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
2020 - Unit 2 contains two plots that have already been discussed, ESR-CB-009 and Trend Plot 7003-
015 which overlap with the Ground Seeded Unit 4. The 2018 reading of the AIM plot and Trend
Plot preceded the unit being planted with sagebrush seedlings. ESR-CB-009 was read in spring
2019 and no seedlings were detected on the plot. This is not entirely a surprise; the seedlings
were planted in an “island” formation on the soil that was mounded. The rationale for doing that
was that the big sagebrush plants pre-fire were located on the mounded soils. Surrounding the
mounds is a shallower, rockier soil, that low sagebrush occupied. It is likely that the random
location of the AIM plot didn’t completely overlap with areas where seedlings were planted in an
island or on mounds. The seedlings were very small so the plot will continue to be read to see if
sagebrush seedlings are detected.
According to research completed by the research scientists at Eastern Oregon Agricultural
Research Center in Unit 2, by the end of the 2019 growing season survival of the seedlings was
an average of 60% survived on the mounded upland soil (88/146, range 33-100% per island) and
61% on the rockier/clayier lower soil (188/145, range 20%-100% per island). Field data was
collected in 2020 and once results are available it will be added to the monitoring report. The
initial season’s survival was promising. The spring of 2020 was drier.

reduce the invasion of undesirable flammable annual plants and to reduce the potential for noxious weeds.

site will be monitored for the establishment of noxious weeds and if found, treated in accordance with
national and district guidelines for noxious weed treatment.
